title: High-fidelity entanglement of polar molecules by dynamic geometric control
authors: Scarlett S. Yu, Avikar Periwal, Jiaqi You, Zirui Liu, Qinshu Lyu, Youngju Cho, Loïc Anderegg, Eunmi Chae, John M. Doyle
abstract: In quantum information systems made of optical tweezer arrays of ultracold molecules, thermal motion of molecules degrades the coherence of their interactions, which limits entanglement fidelity and the concomitant scientific applicability of these systems. We show that by controlling the geometry of the dipolar interaction, even when a molecule occupies many motional states in the tweezer, coherence can be preserved. We characterize several geometries that suppress sensitivity to thermal fluctuations. We further use programmable, coherence-preserving motion of the molecules during entanglement to refocus dephasing from relative positional jitter of the tweezers, which is relevant even on the 10 nm scale. These methods yield substantially improved dipolar coherence and enable generation of two-molecule entanglement with a Bell state fidelity of $\mathcal{F}= 0.976^{+0.008}_{-0.011}$ in directly laser-cooled molecules.
summary: The researchers addressed the challenge of decoherence in polar molecule quantum systems caused by thermal motion within optical tweezer arrays. They developed sophisticated control schemes, including geometric engineering and programmable echo sequences, which successfully suppressed sensitivity to positional jitter. These methods enabled the generation of high-fidelity entanglement ($\mathcal{F} \approx 0.976$), pushing the boundaries for molecular quantum information processing.
main_problem: The coherence of quantum interactions between polar molecules trapped in optical tweezers is degraded by thermal motion and positional fluctuations, limiting entanglement fidelity.
main_result: By employing dynamic geometric control and programmable molecular motion (geometric echo), the authors achieved a high two-molecule Bell state fidelity of $\mathcal{F}= 0.976^{+0.008}_{-0.011}$ in directly laser-cooled molecules.
method: The study uses optical tweezer arrays controlled by SLMs and AODs to engineer the dipolar interaction geometry, combined with advanced quantum control techniques like dynamic decoupling and echo protocols.
model_or_system: The system involves polar molecules (e.g., $	ext{CaF}$) trapped in 2D optical tweezers, whose coherent dynamics are governed by a dipolar coupling Hamiltonian $J$. The methodology focuses on minimizing the sensitivity of this interaction to motional states and positional noise.
key_observables: Entanglement fidelity ($\mathcal{F}$), Dipolar coherence quality factor ($Q$), Single-body coherence time ($	au_{sb}$).
important_parameters: Trap position fluctuations (down to 10 nm scale), Geometric parameters ($	heta, z_0$), Molecular temperature/motional occupation ($ ar{n}$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitations are identified as residual axial positional disorder ($\sigma_z$) and the need for complex site-dependent calibrations across the array.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry control using SLM/AODs, show how geometric engineering minimizes motional sensitivity ($S$), and demonstrate the improvement in coherence quality factor ($Q$) achieved by implementing echo protocols.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying thermal motion as the primary decoherence source to proposing static geometric solutions (magic angles), then advancing to dynamic control via programmable molecular motion (echo protocol) to suppress positional noise, culminating in high-fidelity entanglement measurements.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant experimental demonstration of active quantum error mitigation using mechanical degrees of freedom. The ability to use controlled molecular motion to refocus environmental noise is highly relevant for building scalable quantum simulators and quantum memories.
